name: Continental Drift
statement: The continents were once joined and have since drifted apart across the face of the Earth.
statementAccent: once joined and have since drifted apart
meaning: Continental drift is the hypothesis that Earth's continents have moved over geological time relative to one another, appearing to have once been joined in a single landmass that later fragmented, with the pieces drifting to their present positions. In its original form, put forward by Alfred Wegener, the continents were imagined to move through the oceanic crust, a mechanism now known to be wrong. The idea was substantially correct in its central claim but was rejected for decades and is today absorbed into and superseded by the theory of plate tectonics.
mechanism: Wegener assembled several independent lines of evidence that the continents had once been united in a supercontinent he called Pangaea. He pointed to the complementary fit of coastlines, most strikingly South America nesting into Africa; to matching fossils of land and freshwater species like Mesosaurus and the Glossopteris flora across now-separate continents; to rock formations and mountain belts that line up when the continents are reassembled; and to paleoclimate clues such as ancient glacial deposits now in the tropics and coal now at high latitudes. What he lacked was a force capable of moving continents, the gap that would keep his hypothesis from acceptance.

examples.text: The eastern bulge of South America nests into the western embayment of Africa, the jigsaw fit that most strikingly suggests the two were once joined.
The freshwater reptile Mesosaurus and the seed-fern Glossopteris are found on continents now separated by wide oceans they could not have crossed, evidence the lands were once connected.
Glacial deposits now in warm regions and coal, formed in lush climates, now near the poles make sense only if the continents once sat elsewhere, reassembled around a different pole.

variants.name: The missing mechanism
variants.text: Wegener's proposed forces, a pole-fleeing centrifugal effect and tidal forces, were shown by calculation to be far too weak to move continents, the flaw that led geophysicists to reject the idea.

variants.name: Holmes's convection
variants.text: Arthur Holmes proposed in the interwar years that heat-driven convection in the mantle could move the crust, supplying the mechanism Wegener lacked, though it remained speculative at the time.

whyItMatters: Continental drift is a classic case study in the history and philosophy of science: a hypothesis substantially correct in its central claim, that continents move and were once joined, yet rejected for roughly half a century mainly because its proponent could not supply a convincing mechanism. It illustrates the tension between explanatory evidence and the demand for a cause, the role of the interdisciplinary outsider, since Wegener was a meteorologist challenging geologists, and the eventual triumph of an idea once independent lines of evidence converge.

working.text: read the fit of coastlines, fossils, rocks, and paleoclimate as a single converging case, as Wegener did, not as isolated coincidences.
note that observational evidence alone did not win acceptance; a plausible driving force, mantle-driven plate motion, was needed.
understand the continents as riding on lithospheric plates rather than ploughing through the seafloor, correcting Wegener's picture.

limits: Wegener's mechanism was wrong: he pictured continents ploughing through the oceanic crust, driven by forces too weak to do so, which is why geophysicists led by figures like Harold Jeffreys rejected the hypothesis by around 1930. In the modern understanding continents do not move through oceanic crust but ride passively on rigid lithospheric plates that move over the ductile asthenosphere. Continental drift has thus been subsumed into and superseded by plate tectonics; the phrase survives as a historical label and as a description of the observed phenomenon, but as a standalone theory it is obsolete.
misreadings: Wegener was not the first to notice that the continents fit together; the jigsaw fit was remarked on centuries earlier by Ortelius and others, and his originality lay in synthesising the fit with fossil, geological, and climatic evidence. Continental drift is not the same as modern plate tectonics: drift had continents moving through the seafloor by inadequate forces, while plate tectonics has whole plates, continental and oceanic crust together, moving by mantle-driven processes. And the popular attribution of the idea to Francis Bacon is a persistent overstatement.
origin: Proposed by the German meteorologist and geophysicist Alfred Wegener in lectures in 1912 and developed in his book 'The Origin of Continents and Oceans' (1915), rejected for lack of a mechanism, and vindicated in the 1950s and 1960s through paleomagnetism and seafloor spreading as it was absorbed into plate tectonics.
